title: Cell and nuclear division
summary: How cells divide by mitosis or meiosis followed by cytokinesis, how meiosis halves chromosome number and creates variation, and how errors in division or cell-cycle control cause disease.

keyterms.definition: Division of the cytoplasm of a parent cell between daughter cells; by a contractile actin–myosin ring in animals and a cell plate in plants.
Nuclear division producing two genetically identical nuclei with the same chromosome number as the parent nucleus.
Reduction division: two successive nuclear divisions that halve the chromosome number (diploid to haploid) and produce genetically varied nuclei.
The two identical DNA molecules of a replicated chromosome, held together at the centromere until they separate in anaphase.
Pair of chromosomes, one from each parent, with the same genes in the same sequence but possibly different alleles.
Repeated coiling of DNA wrapped around histones that condenses chromosomes before division, making them shorter, thicker and easier to move.
Protein fibres that attach to centromeres and, with microtubule motor proteins, move chromosomes or chromatids to opposite poles.
Failure of homologous chromosomes or sister chromatids to separate in meiosis, producing gametes with an extra or missing chromosome.
Exchange of DNA between non-sister chromatids of a homologous pair (bivalent) during prophase I, producing new combinations of alleles.
Independent alignment of each bivalent at metaphase I, so the maternal or paternal chromosome of each pair can go to either pole.
Sequence of phases in a dividing cell: interphase (G1, S, G2), then mitosis and cytokinesis.
Proteins whose concentrations rise and fall during the cell cycle; they bind and activate cyclin-dependent kinases, triggering progression to the next phase.
Gene that normally promotes cell-cycle progression; mutation can turn it into an oncogene that drives uncontrolled division.
Gene that normally inhibits cell-cycle progression; loss-of-function mutations remove this brake and can contribute to tumour formation.
Spread of cells from a malignant primary tumour to other parts of the body, where they form secondary tumours.
Number of cells in mitosis divided by the total number of cells observed; a high index indicates rapid cell division, e.g. in tumours.

questions.prompt: How does cytokinesis occur in plant cells?
options: A ring of actin and myosin contracts, pinching the cell in two
Vesicles gather at the equator and fuse to form a cell plate, which becomes a new cell wall
The cell wall folds inwards to form a cleavage furrow
The nucleus divides and the two nuclei push the cytoplasm apart
questions.explanation: A rigid cell wall prevents plant cells from being pinched in two, so a new wall is built from the inside out by a cell plate. Contractile actin–myosin rings are how animal cells divide.

questions.prompt: Put the phases of mitosis in order.
questions.explanation: Chromosomes condense (prophase), line up at the equator (metaphase), have their chromatids pulled apart (anaphase) and are enclosed in new nuclei (telophase).

questions.prompt: Match each phase of mitosis to its key events.

pairs.right: Chromosomes condense and the nuclear membrane breaks down
Chromosomes line up at the equator of the spindle
Sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles
Nuclear membranes re-form and chromosomes decondense

questions.explanation: Each phase has a recognisable chromosome arrangement, which is how phases are identified in micrographs.

questions.statement: DNA replication takes place during prophase of mitosis.
questions.explanation: DNA is replicated before nuclear division begins, during interphase. By prophase each chromosome already consists of two sister chromatids.

questions.text: After DNA replication, each chromosome consists of two identical ___ held together until anaphase.
questions.explanation: Replication produces two identical DNA molecules (chromatids) joined at the centromere. Homologous chromosomes are a maternal–paternal pair, not copies of one molecule.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of unequal cytokinesis?
options: Division of cells in an onion root tip
Division of skin cells during wound healing
Division of cells in a leaf meristem
Budding in yeast
questions.explanation: In budding, a small bud receives much less cytoplasm than the parent cell. Oogenesis is another example: the egg keeps most of the cytoplasm and the polar bodies get very little.

questions.statement: Mitosis produces two genetically identical nuclei with the same number of chromosomes as the parent nucleus.
questions.explanation: Each daughter nucleus receives one chromatid from every chromosome, so chromosome number and genetic content are maintained, as needed for growth, repair and asexual reproduction.

questions.text: Chromosomes condense during prophase by ___, in which DNA wrapped around histones is coiled repeatedly.
questions.explanation: Condensed chromosomes are short and compact, so they can be moved to the poles without tangling or breaking.

questions.prompt: In a micrograph of an onion root tip, a cell shows two groups of V-shaped chromosomes moving towards opposite poles. Which phase is this?
options: Prophase
Anaphase
Metaphase
Telophase
questions.explanation: Separated chromatids are pulled by their centromeres, so the arms trail behind in a V shape as they move to the poles. In telophase the chromosomes have reached the poles and new nuclei form.

questions.prompt: What moves sister chromatids to opposite poles in anaphase?
options: Spindle microtubules attached to the centromeres shorten, pulling the chromatids
A contractile ring of actin and myosin
Cytoplasmic streaming
Repulsion between the negatively charged chromatids
questions.explanation: Spindle microtubules, together with microtubule motor proteins, pull on the centromeres. The actin–myosin ring acts later, in animal cytokinesis.

questions.prompt: A human cell with 46 chromosomes undergoes meiosis. What is produced?
options: Two diploid cells, each with 46 chromosomes
Four haploid cells, each with 46 chromosomes
Two haploid cells, each with 23 chromosomes
Four haploid cells, each with 23 chromosomes
questions.explanation: Meiosis is a reduction division: two divisions after one round of replication give four nuclei, each with one chromosome from every homologous pair (n = 23).

questions.prompt: Put these stages of meiosis in order.
items: Prophase I: homologous chromosomes pair up and cross over
Metaphase I: bivalents line up at the equator
Anaphase I: homologous chromosomes move to opposite poles
Metaphase II: chromosomes line up at the equator of each cell
questions.explanation: Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes (halving the chromosome number); meiosis II separates sister chromatids, much like mitosis.

questions.statement: Sister chromatids separate during anaphase I of meiosis.
questions.explanation: In anaphase I, homologous chromosomes separate and each still has two chromatids. Sister chromatids separate in anaphase II.

questions.text: The exchange of DNA between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes is called ___.
questions.explanation: During prophase I, chromatids of paired homologues break and rejoin, swapping sections. This produces chromatids with new combinations of alleles.

questions.prompt: Match each event to the stage of meiosis in which it occurs.
questions.explanation: The two sources of variation (crossing over and random orientation) both happen in meiosis I; the reduction in chromosome number happens at anaphase I.

questions.prompt: Ignoring crossing over, how many different combinations of chromosomes can random orientation produce in human gametes (n = 23)?
options: 2⁴⁶
2²³
questions.explanation: Each of the 23 bivalents can face either way independently, giving 2 × 2 × ... (23 times) = 2²³, about 8.4 million combinations.

questions.statement: Down syndrome is usually caused by non-disjunction producing a gamete with an extra copy of chromosome 21.
questions.explanation: If chromosome 21 fails to separate in meiosis, a gamete may carry two copies; fertilisation then gives a zygote with three (trisomy 21).

questions.text: The failure of homologous chromosomes or sister chromatids to separate during meiosis is called ___.
questions.explanation: Non-disjunction leaves one gamete with an extra chromosome and another with one missing, changing chromosome number in the offspring.

questions.prompt: What trend is shown by data on the incidence of Down syndrome?
options: The risk increases with maternal age
The risk is the same at all maternal ages
The risk decreases with maternal age
The risk depends only on the father's age
questions.explanation: Data show that the chance of non-disjunction, and so of trisomy 21, rises markedly in older mothers. Correlation data like this are used to counsel parents about risk.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes meiosis from mitosis?
options: Only mitosis is preceded by DNA replication
Meiosis produces cells that are genetically identical to each other
Meiosis involves two divisions and produces genetically different haploid nuclei
Chromosomes condense only in meiosis
questions.explanation: Both divisions need prior DNA replication and both involve chromosome condensation and spindle movement. Meiosis differs by having two divisions, halving the chromosome number and generating variation.

questions.prompt: Put the phases of the cell cycle in order, starting after a cell is formed.
items: G1: cell growth and protein synthesis
G2: further growth and preparation for division
questions.explanation: Interphase (G1, S, G2) is the longest part of the cycle; the cell grows and replicates its DNA before dividing its nucleus and then its cytoplasm.

questions.prompt: Which activity does NOT occur during interphase?
options: DNA replication
Synthesis of proteins
Separation of sister chromatids
Increase in the number of mitochondria
questions.explanation: Interphase is a metabolically active growth phase: biosynthesis, organelle multiplication and DNA replication. Chromatids separate only during anaphase of mitosis.

questions.text: Proteins whose concentrations rise and fall during the cell cycle, and which activate cyclin-dependent kinases, are called ___.
questions.explanation: Each cyclin reaches a threshold at a particular point in the cycle; binding to its kinase then triggers the next phase.

questions.statement: Cyclins bind to cyclin-dependent kinases, which then phosphorylate target proteins that trigger the next stage of the cell cycle.
questions.explanation: Kinases are inactive without their cyclin. Once activated, they add phosphate groups to other proteins, switching on processes such as DNA replication or mitosis.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its description.

pairs.right: Normal gene that stimulates cell-cycle progression
Normal gene that inhibits cell-cycle progression
Spread of cancer cells forming secondary tumours

questions.explanation: Cancer usually needs mutations that both over-activate the 'accelerator' (oncogenes) and disable the 'brakes' (tumour suppressor genes). Malignant tumours can then metastasise.

questions.prompt: In a tissue sample, 48 out of 600 cells are in mitosis. What is the mitotic index?
questions.explanation: Mitotic index = cells in mitosis ÷ total cells = 48 ÷ 600 = 0.08. Tissues with an unusually high mitotic index may indicate a tumour.

questions.statement: Benign tumours invade neighbouring tissues and metastasise to form secondary tumours.
questions.explanation: Benign tumours stay localised and do not invade or spread. Malignant tumours invade nearby tissue and can metastasise, which is what makes them cancerous.

questions.text: The mitotic index is the number of cells in ___ divided by the total number of cells observed.
questions.explanation: Cells in prophase, metaphase, anaphase or telophase are counted; a higher proportion means faster proliferation.

questions.prompt: Why can a mutation in a tumour suppressor gene contribute to cancer?
options: It makes the gene produce an overactive protein that stimulates division
It causes the cell to undergo meiosis instead of mitosis
It removes a protein that normally stops the cell cycle when conditions are not right
It prevents DNA replication in the S phase
questions.explanation: Tumour suppressor proteins act as brakes on the cell cycle; loss-of-function mutations remove that control. An overactive stimulating protein is the effect of an oncogene instead.

questions.prompt: Where would you expect the highest rate of cell proliferation?
options: Mature red blood cells
Neurons in an adult brain
Mature xylem vessels
The apical meristem of a growing root
questions.explanation: Meristems, like early embryos and the basal layer of skin, proliferate for growth and replacement. Red blood cells have no nucleus, xylem vessels are dead and adult neurons rarely divide.
